newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan celebrates bitter-sweet golden jubilee.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan celebrates bitter-sweet golden jubilee.

text.p: Amid fireworks and flags, Pakistan ushered in its 50th anniversary of independence on Thursday with Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif calling for the nation to work for the prosperity of future generations.

"Let's make a pledge today that we will not only look towards ourselves and the present, but the objective of our efforts and performance will be the creation of a developed and prosperous Pakistan for our coming generations," he declared.

Sharif, addressing the National Assembly (lower house) at one minute past midnight, said the political bitterness of the past should be set aside and urged the opposition to help start a new era of development and progress.
He was speaking only hours after Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party walked out of parliamentary sessions at which the government pushed through a sweeping new anti-terrorism bill.

The bill, which needs only presidential assent to become law, is designed to combat a wave of violence involving Sunni and Shi'ite militants in the populous province of Punjab, as well as ethnic unrest in the southern port city of Karachi.

Despite their country's economic and political woes, many ordinary Pakistanis took to the streets at midnight to let off firecrackers and cheer the anniversary of August 14, 1947, when Pakistan and India won their independence from British rule.
Sharif's brother, Punjab province chief minister Shahbaz Sharif, led a big rally in the city of Rawalpindi, near the capital Islamabad, with a fireworks display after midnight.

The prime minister, flanked by cabinet ministers, diplomats and other dignitaries, attended a flag-raising ceremony outside Parliament in Islamabad at eight a.m. (0300 GMT). He was due to lay a wreath at the memorial to national poet Allama Iqbal in Lahore later in the day and then fly to Karachi for a rally at the mausoleum of Pakistan's founder Mohammad Ali Jinnah, always referred to here as Qaid-e-Azam (great leader).

But official celebrations were low-key, with no military parades or lavish events, reflecting a mood of introspection and austerity in a country grappling with sectarian violence and searching for a way out of a chronic economic crisis.

"State institutions and the infrastructure are crumbling, lawlessness threatens society, the debt trap is daunting and the economy is in dire straits," the English-language daily The News said in an editorial on Thursday. "Government credibility and faith in its ability to turn things around is very low."

"Despite the general cynicism and despondency that overshadow the celebrations...Pakistan is not about to collapse," the newspaper said. "It is inherently viable and vibrant enough to belie those who declare it a failed state."
